<reason>Both sides were excellent, disciplined, and highly responsive, with clean Q1/Q2 and A1/A2 structure and no fake sourcing. CON built a sharp case: every licensing lever presupposes detection, unverifiable claims are safer as disclosure than as a certificate, and industry-written thresholds mean capture. But PRO won the decisive pressure exchange: B3.1 forced A4.1's concession ("None") that the risk-based status quo detects no frontier misrepresentation either, and B4.5-B4.6 converted CON's central epistemic weapon into a symmetrical indictment that licensing at least meets with a gate. PRO's burden-inversion reframe (doubt defaults to "not yet," so the regulator need not prove violations ex ante) directly answered the day-one-threshold question, and "license the release decision itself" gave a genuine third horn to the open-weight dilemma that CON's leakage counter only partially dented (leakage afflicts CON's regime worse — no unlawful act at all). CON kept entrenchment, capture, and geofencing alive, and PRO's answers there were thin (partly because two of PRO's turns were clipped — a real execution cost that keeps the margin small). But CON's escapes established parity-of-blindness rather than superiority of the status quo, while PRO's frame — who bears the cost of uncertainty for irreversible harms — survived as the cleaner decision rule and was crystallized more decisively in the closing.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>PRO's Q1 (B3.1) demanding CON name one misrepresentation the risk-based regime catches that licensing misses, drawing A4.1's "None," then B4.5-B4.6 turning CON's "regulators can't verify" weapon against the status quo — the pivotal concession of the debate. Runner-up: B4.3's "license the release decision" answer dissolving CON's open-weight ban-or-exempt dilemma.</best_rebuttal>
